sentences.text: The holotype specimen of Baryonyx was estimated to be between 7.5 and 10 meters long and weigh between 1.2 and 2 metric tons.
This predator possessed robust forelimbs featuring a first-finger claw measuring approximately 31 centimeters in length.
Estimates place the animal at 2.5 meters in hip height, with a skull length of 91 to 95 centimeters.
The fused sternum of the holotype suggests that the individual may have been mature.
Amateur fossil collector William J. Walker discovered the initial remains in January 1983 at the Smokejack Clay Pit in Surrey, England.
The first complete skeleton was found in the same location during that year.
Walker donated the claw to the Natural History Museum, while the Ockley Brick Company donated the rest of the skeleton and equipment.
It took six years of constant preparation to extract all the bones from the rock matrix of the holotype specimen.
Palaeontologists Alan J. Charig and Angela C. Milner formally named the animal in 1986.
Baryonyx was the first theropod dinosaur proven to be piscivorous, based on fish scales found in the stomach region of the holotype.
Researchers suggest that Baryonyx may have had semi-aquatic habits.
Baryonyx is classified as a member of the family Spinosauridae.
The genus belongs to the subfamily Baryonychinae.
It is part of the superfamily Megalosauroidea.
Baryonyx lived during the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 130 to 125 million years ago.
This creature inhabited what is now Europe during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 130 to 125 million years ago in the Aptian stage.

It is debated whether Suchosaurus cultridens is a senior synonym of Baryonyx and whether Suchomimus tenerensis belongs in the same genus, with some researchers suggesting they are synonyms while others keep them separate.
In 2019, Thomas M. S. Arden and colleagues concluded that a Portuguese skeleton previously attributed to Baryonyx did not belong to the genus because its dentary bone was not strongly upturned.
In 2024, Erik Isasmendi and colleagues concluded that no spinosaurid specimens from Iberia could be assigned to Baryonyx.
In 2002, Hans-Dieter Sues and colleagues proposed that Suchomimus tenerensis was a species of Baryonyx and that Suchomimus was identical to Cristatusaurus.
